content: Coronaviruses are a large family of viruses capable of causing a spectrum of illnesses in humans, ranging from mild conditions like the common cold to severe diseases such as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS). These viruses are also known to infect a variety of animal species. In late 2012, a novel coronavirus, previously unrecognized in humans, was identified in a resident of the Middle East. This virus, now referred to as the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV), has, as of May 4, 2018, resulted in over 2,206 laboratory-confirmed cases of human infection. All individuals infected with MERS-CoV to date have had either direct or indirect links to the Middle East. However, limited human-to-human transmission has been documented in other countries, primarily involving individuals who had recently traveled to the Middle East. The majority of MERS-CoV cases have presented with respiratory disease, though secondary complications such as acute renal failure, multi-organ failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and disseminated intravascular coagulation have also been reported. Additionally, some patients have experienced gastrointestinal symptoms, including diarrhea. The case fatality rate is approximately 36%. Most laboratory-confirmed cases have involved individuals with at least one pre-existing comorbidity, although many cases have occurred in previously healthy individuals. Current evidence suggests that MERS-CoV is a zoonotic virus that has entered human populations in the Arabian Peninsula multiple times, likely through direct or indirect contact with infected dromedary camels or camel-related products. Studies have demonstrated that MERS-CoV-specific antibodies are widespread in dromedary camel populations in the Middle East and Africa. Serological surveys in animals suggest that MERS-CoV has been circulating in camels for decades. However, the reasons for the emergence of human cases in 2012 remain unclear, and the specific exposures and transmission mechanisms from animals to humans have not been fully elucidated. Human-to-human transmission of MERS-CoV has been observed to a limited extent within households. However, the majority of human cases reported to date have resulted from transmission in healthcare settings. Failures in infection prevention and control measures in healthcare environments have occasionally led to large numbers of secondary cases, as seen in Saudi Arabia in April-May 2014 and in South Korea in May-July 2015. To date, there is no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed standardized guidelines to assist public health authorities and investigators in planning and conducting investigations around confirmed and probable cases of MERS-CoV infection. These guidelines are intended to be used in conjunction with other detailed resources, such as laboratory testing protocols and study methodologies. The document is updated as necessary to reflect advancements in the understanding of MERS-CoV transmission and control. The primary objectives of these investigations include identifying additional cases, detecting human-to-human transmission, reducing further spread of the virus, and implementing appropriate prevention and control measures. Investigations also aim to describe the epidemiology, clinical characteristics, and virology of cases, as well as to identify potential sources of exposure and risk factors for infection. Enhanced surveillance and active case finding are critical components of these efforts. In countries where MERS-CoV infections are believed to have originated from animal or environmental sources, investigations focus on identifying the exposures that result in human infection. In countries with secondary transmission related to imported cases, the emphasis is on identifying secondary cases and monitoring for community transmission. Early detection of cases relies heavily on the awareness of healthcare providers and the availability of mechanisms for reporting suspected cases. The WHO emphasizes the importance of assembling multidisciplinary teams for investigations, including experts in epidemiology, clinical assessment, laboratory diagnostics, infection prevention and control, and risk communication. Animal health specialists are also integral to these teams. Investigations should begin promptly upon laboratory confirmation of a MERS-CoV case, although they may need to commence earlier if laboratory results are delayed. Data collection during investigations should include detailed demographic, clinical, and epidemiological information. This includes the patient’s travel history, potential animal and human exposures, clinical presentation, and outcomes. Laboratory data, including virological testing and ancillary investigations such as imaging, should also be systematically recorded. Infection control measures implemented in healthcare settings should be documented to assess potential breaches. Case definitions for identifying additional cases should be developed locally and tailored to the specific context of the outbreak. These definitions should be sensitive enough to capture the majority of cases during the early stages of an investigation. Retrospective case finding should also be conducted to identify potential exposures and transmission chains. In summary, the effective management of MERS-CoV outbreaks requires a coordinated approach involving early detection, rapid response, and comprehensive data collection. Awareness among healthcare providers and adherence to infection prevention and control measures are critical to limiting the spread of the virus and reducing morbidity and mortality.
